To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the LDH and PK isozyme patterns are different between dystrophic and nondystrophic animals in the kidney, thigh muscle, and heart at different stages of development; 2) the LDH isoenzymes are expressed at different levels in the heart and thigh muscle of dystrophic mice; 3) the LDH expression pattern is similar in the thigh muscle and heart; 4) the LDH pattern is different in the heart and skeletal muscle; and 5
dystrophic mice exhibit altered LDH and PK expression, which are tissue specific and temporally regulated.

(1) dystrophic mice (dy2J/+) have a lower LDH and PK enzyme activity in the thigh muscle (MD) compared to the nondystrophic mice (dy+/+); (2) this genotype difference in LDH activity is also observed in kidney, whereas in the heart, the PK enzyme activity is higher in dystrophic mice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the molecular mechanisms of MD and the development of a model of the human condition.
the study of the regulation of the LDH and PK isozymes in the mouse model of muscular dystrophy.
the identification of the dystrophin gene, and the elucidation of the biochemical mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of MD.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the dy2J mutation is a regulator of the expression of LDH and PK in C57BL6 mice.
the dystrophic mutation affects the regulation of LDH and PK in C57BL/dy2J mice.

the dystrophic mutation affects the temporal and tissue specific regulation of the expression of LDH and PK, and that this effect may be related to the pleiotropic action of this locus during the development of the MD condition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the dy2J mutation affects the regulation of LDH and PK in C57BL6/J mice.
the dy2J gene is responsible for a pleiotropic effect on the expression of several genes involved in the regulation of the metabolism of energy substrates.
the dy2J gene is a pleiotropic gene, affecting the regulation of several genes in the MD pathway.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dystrophic phenotype of dy2J mice is not a simple result of the absence of the dy2 protein, but a consequence of the pleiotropic effects of this gene.
the dystrophic mutation affects not only the muscle but also other tissues, and that this pleiotropy may have a role in the etiology of the disease.
the dy2J mutation is not only responsible for the MD phenotype but also for the temporal regulation of the enzymes LDH and PK in the tissues affected by the disease.
